Round 1 / Speaker: Alice Statement: Hi Sophie,

I’d like to start by saying that I still think the group should adopt Principle 1 – Maximizing Floor Income as our collective choice.

Why the floor matters most right now

1. Risk‑aversion under high stakes – In Phase II the payoff will be much larger, but we have no idea how the final distribution will look. If we pick a principle that only maximizes the average, the “pie” could be very uneven and some of us could end up with a very low draw. A floor constraint guarantees that everyone receives at least a decent minimum, protecting us from a disastrous outcome.

2. The experiment’s framing – The whole study emphasizes that lifetime income is largely a matter of luck and accidents. A rule that explicitly safeguards the worst‑off aligns with that moral narrative and with the idea that society should compensate for those random disadvantages.

3. Efficiency vs. equity trade‑off – Even if a pure‑average‑maximizing rule could raise total surplus, the loss of the floor could outweigh any gain because the variance would be higher. By imposing a floor we still allow the average to be as high as possible *subject* to that minimum, so we do not sacrifice all efficiency—just enough to ensure a safety net for everyone.

4. Strategic leverage – A floor constraint narrows the set of admissible distributions. That forces any designer of the final draw to respect a baseline level, which should raise the worst possible payoff for each of us.

I’m confident that this principle balances fairness with a reasonable level of overall earnings, and it reflects the ethical intuition that we should protect the most vulnerable members of the group—including ourselves.

I’d love to hear your thoughts. Do you see any reason to favor a different principle, or any concerns about the floor approach? If you’re open to it, I think we can move quickly to a vote after we’ve exchanged viewpoints.
Round 1 / Speaker: Sophie Statement: Hi Alice and everyone,

Thanks for laying out such a clear case for Principle 1 – Maximizing Floor Income. I’m completely on board with you.

Why I’m also leaning toward the floor‑maximizing rule

1. Consistent with my own ranking – In Phase I I placed the floor principle at the top of my list (and was “sure” about it). The four individual application rounds reinforced that I value guaranteeing the highest possible income for the poorest class above any gain in average earnings.

2. Empirical support from my rounds – In each of the four demo rounds I chose distributions that maximized the floor, even when that meant a slightly lower personal payoff. The fact that I was willing to accept a $1.70 payoff (Round 2) rather than a higher one shows how strongly I prioritize the worst‑off.

3. Risk‑aversion under uncertainty – As you noted, the final draw in Phase II will involve much larger stakes. By fixing a strong floor we protect everyone from a disastrous low outcome, which feels especially important given that the experiment frames income as largely a matter of luck.

4. Fairness narrative – The study’s premise is that many income differences are accidental. A rule that explicitly lifts the lowest income class aligns with that moral framing and with the intuition that society should compensate for random disadvantages.

5. No major efficiency sacrifice – Maximizing the floor does not preclude a high average; it simply restricts the set of admissible distributions to those that keep the poorest above a decent threshold. In practice this still leaves room for a substantial overall surplus.

I can’t think of any compelling reason to shift to a constrained‑average principle (3 or 4) or to pure average maximization (2). Those alternatives would lower the guaranteed minimum for the worst‑off, which conflicts with both my personal ranking and the ethical story of the experiment.

Next step  
If everyone else feels the same, I suggest we move straight to a vote on Principle 1. We can keep the discussion brief—if anyone has a new point or a strong objection, let’s hear it now; otherwise I’m happy to cast my vote for the floor‑maximizing rule.

Looking forward to hearing from the rest of the group!
